stories.teaser: A $60 Israeli blood test spots lung cancer with 93% accuracy
stories.headline: A $60 Israeli blood test spots stage 2–4 lung cancer with 93% accuracy
stories.why: Peer-reviewed study of 103 participants: 93% of stage 2–4 cancers found, 90% of healthy people correctly cleared.
texts:
Imagine catching lung cancer with a simple blood test.

Researchers at Tel Aviv University, working with doctors at Bnai Zion and Sheba Medical Centers, built a $60 test that reads chemical changes in DNA fragments in the blood. In a study of 103 people, it found 93% of stage 2–4 lung cancers.

“If we can discover the disease in its early stages, we can go to surgery,” says oncologist Dr. Abed Agbarya.

#Israel #Science #CancerResearch #Health

93% accuracy. $60. One blood sample.

In a peer-reviewed study of 103 participants, an Israeli blood test identified 93% of stage 2–4 lung cancers and correctly ruled out cancer in 90% of healthy people. It was developed at Tel Aviv University with JaxBio Technologies, Bnai Zion and Sheba Medical Centers. A larger trial is now underway in Israel and Europe.

#Israel #Science #CancerResearch #Health

What if finding lung cancer early took just a blood draw?

Tel Aviv University’s Dr. Yuval Ebenstein and his partners created a glass chip that makes chemical changes in tumor DNA light up, with no DNA sequencing needed. In a study of 103 people, the $60 test caught 93% of stage 2–4 lung cancers. A larger trial in Israel and Europe runs through mid-2027.

#Israel #Science #CancerResearch #Health
stories.og_title: $60 Israeli blood test can detect stage 2-4 lung cancer with 93% accuracy, study shows

stories.teaser: FDA clears an Israeli app that helps adjust insulin doses
stories.headline: FDA clears Israeli app that gives people with diabetes personalized insulin doses
stories.why: DreaMed Diabetes’ MODI app, born at Schneider Children’s Medical Center, received U.S. FDA clearance.
texts:
For people living with diabetes, getting the insulin dose right can be a daily worry.

Israeli company DreaMed Diabetes just received U.S. FDA clearance for MODI, an app for adults with type 2 diabetes. It analyzes glucose levels and insulin data and gives personalized dosing recommendations between doctor visits. The technology grew out of research at Schneider Children’s Medical Center.

#Israel #HealthTech #Diabetes #Innovation

FDA clearance for an Israeli app that helps people with type 2 diabetes adjust their insulin.

DreaMed Diabetes’ MODI analyzes glucose patterns and treatment data and recommends personalized insulin doses, without a doctor approving each change. More than 8 million people in the U.S. use insulin injections. The company’s 30 employees are all based in Israel.

#Israel #HealthTech #Diabetes #Innovation

What if your insulin dose could be fine-tuned between doctor visits?

That’s what MODI, from Israel’s DreaMed Diabetes, does. The newly FDA-cleared app turns glucose and insulin data into personalized dosing advice for adults with type 2 diabetes.

“Information alone does not improve patients’ health,” says CEO Eran Atlas. “The value is created when it is turned into a personalized recommendation that arrives at the right time.”

#Israel #HealthTech #Diabetes #Innovation
stories.og_title: Israeli app for adjusting insulin dosage receives FDA approval

stories.teaser: 2,000-year-old pilgrims’ purification complex found in Jerusalem
stories.headline: Archaeologists uncover a 2,000-year-old pilgrims’ purification complex in Jerusalem
stories.why: Three ritual baths, a 12 by 9.5 meter pool and a paved plaza, dated from the 1st century BCE to 70 CE.
texts:
Picture the pilgrims who came to Jerusalem 2,000 years ago.

Hebrew University archaeologists have uncovered where many of them likely purified themselves before visiting the Temple: three large ritual baths, a plastered pool about 12 by 9.5 meters, a paved plaza and a drainage system. One ritual bath still stands to its full height of 4.2 meters, stone vault and all.

#Israel #Archaeology #Jerusalem #History

3 ritual baths. A 12 by 9.5 meter pool. About 280 square meters, in use from the 1st century BCE until 70 CE.

That’s the purification complex Prof. Uzi Leibner and Prof. Orit Peleg-Barkat of the Hebrew University uncovered at the Ophel in Jerusalem. Its location and scale suggest it served large numbers of Jewish pilgrims.

#Israel #Archaeology #Jerusalem #History

Where did ancient pilgrims prepare before entering the Temple?

Hebrew University archaeologists may have found the answer at the Ophel in Jerusalem: a monumental complex of ritual baths and a large stepped pool.

“A monumental ashlar structure devoted entirely to ritual purification, situated at the foot of the Temple Mount and near one of its gates, is a truly unparalleled phenomenon,” say Prof. Uzi Leibner and Prof. Orit Peleg-Barkat.

#Israel #Archaeology #Jerusalem #History
stories.og_title: Second Temple-era purification complex uncovered near Temple Mount

stories.teaser: Israeli doctors treat about 200 patients a day in Panama City
stories.headline: Israeli medical team treats about 200 patients a day in a poor Panama City neighborhood
stories.why: Ichilov Hospital’s aid team, plus 28 young Israeli volunteers, also donated 200 pairs of eyeglasses.
texts:
Some of the best diplomacy happens in a clinic.

A medical team from Tel Aviv’s Ichilov Hospital set up in El Chorrillo, a poor neighborhood of Panama City, treating about 200 patients each day. Alongside them, 28 young Israelis fresh out of the army taught at local schools and renovated classrooms and clinics.

“We go everywhere in the world — in Asia, Africa and Latin America — and bring the help that local residents need,” says Dr. Ronit Almog.

#Israel #Panama #GlobalHealth #Volunteering

About 200 patients a day. 200 pairs of eyeglasses donated. 28 young volunteers.

That’s what an Israeli delegation from Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center (Ichilov) brought to El Chorrillo, a poor neighborhood of Panama City. The doctors worked alongside Panamanian colleagues, while volunteers from Heroes for Life taught in local schools and renovated school facilities and clinics.

#Israel #Panama #GlobalHealth #Volunteering

What does friendship between countries look like up close?

In Panama City, it looked like Israeli doctors from Ichilov Hospital treating about 200 patients a day in the struggling El Chorrillo neighborhood, and young Israeli volunteers teaching kids and fixing up their schools.

“This mission is much more than medical aid — it is an expression of the friendship between Israel and Panama,” says Israel’s ambassador, Mattanya Cohen.

#Israel #Panama #GlobalHealth #Volunteering
stories.og_title: 'Diplomacy that reaches people': Israeli medical team brings aid to Panama City

stories.teaser: A volunteer doctor at a Jerusalem pop-up clinic spots a stroke
stories.headline: At a Jerusalem pop-up clinic, a volunteer doctor spotted a grandfather’s stroke
stories.why: United Hatzalah’s mobile clinic: physicians, paramedics and four treatment beds, open 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. over Sukkot.
texts:
A grandfather brought his grandson in for a minor injury. He left with his own life possibly saved.

At United Hatzalah’s mobile clinic in Jerusalem, he mentioned headaches to a volunteer physician, who recognized early signs of a stroke and sent him straight to the hospital. The clinic, set up outside the Jerusalem International YMCA, cared for visitors over Sukkot.

#Israel #UnitedHatzalah #Jerusalem #SavingLives

Physicians and paramedics, four treatment beds, open 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. through the Sukkot holiday.

United Hatzalah’s Ruderman Mobile Emergency Care Clinic on King David Street in Jerusalem treated visitors close to the Old City and major hotels. In one case, a volunteer physician recognized early stroke symptoms in a grandfather who came in with his grandson, and he was rushed to the hospital.

#Israel #UnitedHatzalah #Jerusalem #SavingLives

Ever wondered what happens if you get sick on a trip to Jerusalem?

Over Sukkot, United Hatzalah parked a mobile emergency clinic just steps from the Old City. One visitor came in for his grandson’s minor injury; a volunteer doctor noticed early stroke signs in him and got him to the hospital.

“Sukkot brings visitors from around the world to Jerusalem, and we want them to know that accessible medical care is close at hand if they need it,” says Jay Ruderman.

#Israel #UnitedHatzalah #Jerusalem #SavingLives
stories.og_title: Mobile emergency clinic offers care to Jerusalem tourists over Sukkot

stories.teaser: Hundreds of Israeli teens spend their holiday sprucing up Kiryat Shmona
stories.headline: Hundreds of Israeli teens spent their holiday break restoring Kiryat Shmona
stories.why: Hashomer Hachadash youth camped in the city all week, painting, clearing debris and cleaning streams.
texts:
How would you spend your school holiday?

Hundreds of teens from the Hashomer Hachadash youth movement spent theirs in Kiryat Shmona, camping at a local campsite and heading out every morning to paint, clear debris and brush, clean streams and beautify the city in Israel’s north.

“Hashomer Hachadash has always been the first to arrive and volunteer across our city,” says Mayor Avichai Stern.

#Israel #Volunteering #Youth #Community

Hundreds of teens. One week. One city.

Over the Sukkot break, young volunteers from Hashomer Hachadash camped in Kiryat Shmona and spent their days painting, clearing debris and brush, and cleaning public spaces, nature sites and streams. Leadership program participants, pre-military academy students, and employees with their families joined them during the holiday week.

#Israel #Volunteering #Youth #Community

This is what the next generation looks like.

Instead of a lazy holiday, hundreds of Israeli teens from Hashomer Hachadash spent Sukkot in Kiryat Shmona, helping a northern city recover from hard years. They camped together, then spent each day painting, clearing brush and cleaning streams and public spaces.

A local farmer says the movement is “always the first to ask, take an interest, and help us.”

#Israel #Volunteering #Youth #Community
stories.og_title: Hashomer Hachadash Youth Dedicate Sukkot to Rehabilitating Communities in Northern Israel

stories.teaser: Israel’s endangered softshell turtles have a record nesting year
stories.headline: Israel’s critically endangered softshell turtles are making a record comeback
stories.why: More than 160 nests this season, up from 77–113 a year between 2018 and 2025.
texts:
Some good news from Israel’s streams: the softshell turtles are coming back.

This critically endangered species had 77 to 113 nests a year in Israel between 2018 and 2025. This season, conservationists counted more than 160, thanks to fences and guards protecting the nesting sites.

“We are also suddenly seeing egg-laying in places where we had never seen it before,” says Dr. Dana Milstein of the Israel Nature and Parks Authority.

#Israel #Nature #Conservation #Wildlife

160+ nests. A record year for one of the Mediterranean’s most endangered turtles.

Israel recorded 77 to 113 softshell turtle nests a year between 2018 and 2025. This season it passed 160. At Nahal Na’aman alone, nests rose from about 10 a season to more than 60, after the Israel Nature and Parks Authority stepped up protection with fencing and guarding.

#Israel #Nature #Conservation #Wildlife

What does it take to save a turtle that can live more than 50 years?

In Israel: fences, guards and restored streams. The result is a record season for the critically endangered softshell turtle, with more than 160 nests.

“In the past, there were about 10 nests there per season, and today we have passed 60 nests,” says ecologist Dr. Dana Milstein about Nahal Na’aman.

#Israel #Nature #Conservation #Wildlife
stories.og_title: Against the odds, Israel's endangered softshell turtles are making a comeback

stories.teaser: Paying attention to pain helped 90% of people heal faster
stories.headline: Paying attention to pain helped nearly 90% of people heal faster, Israeli study finds
stories.why: Bar-Ilan University study of 57 people, published in Nature Human Behaviour.
texts:
Next time something hurts, maybe don’t look away.

Researchers at Bar-Ilan University gave 57 volunteers a small skin inflammation. Those who focused on it, rather than watching distracting videos, healed better: nearly 90% showed reduced inflammation, with swelling and redness about 1.5 times smaller.

“Feeling pain does contribute to the healing process,” says Dr. Liron Rozenkrantz.

#Israel #Science #Health #MindBody

Nearly 90% showed less inflammation, just by paying attention.

In a Bar-Ilan University study of 57 people aged 20 to 45, participants who focused on a small skin inflammation had swelling and redness about 1.5 times smaller than those who were distracted. The study, with Emek Medical Center, was published in Nature Human Behaviour.

#Israel #Science #Health #MindBody

Can your mind help your body heal?

A Bar-Ilan University study says yes. When 57 volunteers focused on a small skin inflammation instead of distracting themselves, nearly 90% saw it shrink more.

“I’ve studied humans for more than 20 years, and this was the most striking effect I’ve ever seen,” says Dr. Liron Rozenkrantz.

#Israel #Science #Health #MindBody
stories.og_title: Feel the burn: 90% of people heal faster by focusing on their pain — Israeli study

stories.teaser: People in Israel were harvesting grain 15,000 years ago
stories.headline: Stone blades show people in Israel were cultivating grain 15,000 years ago
stories.why: University of Haifa study of 158 flint sickle blades, published in Scientific Reports.
texts:
Farming may have started earlier than we thought, and right here in Israel.

University of Haifa researchers studied 158 flint sickle blades under a microscope. The wear marks show the Natufians, who lived about 15,000 years ago, harvested wild cereals over several weeks and at different stages of ripening.

The Natufians “knew how to identify and exploit non-shattering varieties,” says Dr. Iris Groman-Yaroslavski.

#Israel #Archaeology #History #Science

158 flint blades. 15,000 years. About 4,500 years before domesticated grain.

University of Haifa researchers examined sickle blades from el-Wad Cave terrace in the Carmel and the Salibiya I site at up to 200 times magnification. The wear marks point to an early form of cereal cultivation by the Natufians. Published in Scientific Reports.

#Israel #Archaeology #History #Science

Who were the first farmers?

A University of Haifa study suggests the Natufians, who lived in the Land of Israel some 15,000 years ago, were already harvesting wild cereals in a planned, sustained way. Microscopic wear on 158 flint sickle blades reveals the story, thousands of years before established agriculture.

#Israel #Archaeology #History #Science
stories.og_title: The Natufians Developed a Sophisticated Harvesting Technique for Wild Cereals as Early as 15,000 years ago

stories.teaser: Good news for fish farms: carp relatives rarely spread a deadly virus
stories.headline: Hebrew University study finds carp’s relatives rarely spread a deadly fish virus
stories.why: Goldfish, grass, silver and black carp proved poor carriers of koi herpesvirus. Published in Aquaculture.
texts:
Here’s some good news for the fish on your holiday table.

Koi herpesvirus can wipe out whole populations of common carp within days. A Hebrew University team led by Prof. Lior David found that the carp’s close relatives (goldfish, grass carp, silver carp and black carp) strongly resist it.

“They are actually very poor at spreading the disease,” he says.

#Israel #Science #Agriculture #FoodSecurity

4 species of farmed fish, and good news for all of them.

Hebrew University researchers tested whether goldfish, grass carp, silver carp and black carp spread koi herpesvirus, which can wipe out common carp populations within days. Only a small fraction got infected, and they spread the disease poorly. These fish are among the world’s most important farmed species. Published in Aquaculture.

#Israel #Science #Agriculture #FoodSecurity

Could a fish virus threaten food supplies around the world?

Koi herpesvirus devastates common carp. But Hebrew University’s Prof. Lior David found that its close relatives rarely pass it on.

“Our results show that, although they can occasionally become infected, they are actually very poor at spreading the disease,” he says. That’s reassuring for fish farms that feed billions.

#Israel #Science #Agriculture #FoodSecurity
stories.og_title: This Rosh Hashanah, the Carp on Your Table Comes with Some Good News
